title: Pandit Girdhari Holds a Meeting
body: Pandit Girdhari Lal, pleader and Congress man, gives notice of a public meeting upon the salt tax, self-rule, and — so runs the police abstract — ‘the general condition of things.’ The Superintendent wants it stopped. ‘Nothing but talk, sahib,’ says the Court Inspector, laying down the file, ‘but talk carries in the hot weather.’ The law, inconveniently, is on the Pandit's side.

choices.label: Ban the meeting under Section 144. Order is order.
choices.outcome: There is no meeting. There is instead a banned meeting, which does more for the Congress cause than any two hours of the Pandit's oratory. He sends round a note of thanks in his beautiful court-hand. You do not think he is joking.

choices.label: Permit it, and send a clerk to take dull notes.
choices.outcome: Nothing happens. The Pandit speaks for two hours in the dust of the maidan, the crowd claps in the right places and goes home to its dinner, and the clerk's notes fill three pages with nothing a prosecutor could love.

choices.label: Attend personally and sit in the front row.
choices.outcome: The sight of the Magistrate in the front row throws the Pandit clean off his stride, and the speech turns courteous on the wing. ‘We are honoured,’ he says afterwards, and means at least half of it. Each of you goes home certain the evening was his.

consult.opinion: ‘Stop it under 144, and stop it to-night,’ says the Superintendent, who scents the non-co-operation movement in any gathering above four. ‘Talk is how the swaraj men build a district into a crowd. Ban the meeting and there is nothing to report.’ He holds that a thing prevented is a thing that never lived. The Pandit, banned, will send you a note of thanks in his best court-hand.

title: Lala Hukum Chand Pays a Call
body: Lala Hukum Chand — moneylender, landholder, holder of half the district's paper — comes to pay his respects, with a basket of Langra mangoes still cool from the well. ‘A trifle of the season,’ he says. Then, folding his hands, he touches on a land suit now before your court, which might with one word be settled ‘to everyone's satisfaction.’

choices.label: Accept the mangoes; ignore the hint.
choices.outcome: The mangoes are excellent. The hint goes home unanswered, and the Lala bows himself out admiring your honesty and doubting your wits. He will come again, with something better than fruit.

choices.label: Decline the mangoes and the man, coldly.
choices.outcome: The basket goes back untouched on the servant's head. The Lala's rupee turns every wheel between here and the river, and from this week the wheels turn stiff. Things move slower in the cutcherry now, and no clerk can tell you why.

choices.label: Have the mangoes; drop a helpful word in court.
choices.outcome: The suit goes the Lala's way, and the mango-stones go out with the sweepings. Nothing is written; nothing need be. The first thread weighs less than a hair, as he well knows.

consult.opinion: ‘Eat the mangoes and thank him warmly — refuse them and you make an enemy who holds half the district’s paper,’ says the Treasury Officer, tallying as he talks. ‘But his word in your court is another article. Hukum Chand does not lend; he invests. Whatever you sign for him this season he will present again next, at compound interest.’ He has watched two magistrates learn the rate.

title: Deputy Collector Mukherjee Is Right Again
body: Sub-Deputy Collector Mukherjee — Cambridge, gold spectacles, and manners too good ever to show that he is the cleverer man — lays a tracing on your desk. ‘If the levels are as the amin took them,’ he says gently, ‘the new drain will put the water into the weavers' quarter, not out of it.’ The levels are as the amin took them. He is right.

choices.label: Thank him publicly and change the scheme.
choices.outcome: The scheme is redrawn and the quarter stays dry. In the vernacular office it is noted that the Magistrate took correction from a Bengali deputy before them all, and the noting is put by for whatever use it may one day serve.

choices.label: Change the scheme; take the credit yourself.
choices.outcome: The quarter stays dry, and the credit comes to your desk. Mukherjee wipes his spectacles and says nothing at all. He is a very patient man.

choices.label: Overrule him. A sahib does not reverse himself before the office.
choices.outcome: The rains prove Mukherjee right to the inch. The weavers' quarter goes under a foot of grey water, and you stand on the bund at dawn watching the charpoys float out of doorways.

consult.who: An old hand at the Club
consult.opinion: ‘Take a Bengali baboo’s correction, before the office?’ The old hand sets down his peg, scandalised. ‘My dear fellow, no. Prestige holds a district — let the deputy put you right once and you may as well hand him your seals. Change the drain if you must, but take the credit.’ His bungalow stands on high ground; he has never watched the weavers’ quarter take the water.

title: The Long Evening
body: Nine o'clock. The punkah has stopped — the punkah-coolie asleep over his rope — and the bungalow is a barn of hot shadow with one lamp, one bottle of Scotch, and eleven hundred miles between you and anyone who knew you before India. A jackal cries somewhere beyond the compound wall. The bottle, at least, is company.

choices.label: Pour a large one. And another. It is that or the silence.
choices.outcome: The second peg is better than the first, and the room grows kinder. Every station keeps the memory of a man who began this way — no scandal, only a nightcap that came a little earlier each hot weather. He was good company too, they say.

choices.label: Pour a small one and write letters home you won't post.
choices.outcome: You write of an India that does not exist to people who could not credit the one that does. It steadies the hand. The letter goes into the drawer with the others, unposted.

choices.label: Go to bed sober and lie awake in the heat.
choices.outcome: You lie under the dead punkah and listen to the brain-fever bird going up the scale till two. At six you are at your desk, sober and hollow-eyed, and the office calls it devotion to duty.

consult.opinion: ‘I have signed the certificates,’ says the Civil Surgeon, not unkindly. ‘The liver, or the revolver, or the slow way — and the slow way starts here, with the peg that keeps the silence off.’ He will not preach abstinence; he is too old a hand. ‘Take a small one and put the bottle across the room. It is the reaching that ruins a man, not the drink.’

title: A New Form Is Required
body: Simla, in its wisdom, sends down Form XIV-B, to be filled in quintuplicate, showing the caste, calling, and ‘general disposition’ of every petitioner appearing before the court. Ram Autar, your head clerk, lays it on the desk and steps back a pace. ‘It is hukm,’ he says, in the flat voice he keeps for orders that are both compulsory and mad.

choices.label: Implement it fully. An order is an order.
choices.outcome: The office goes under quintuplicate like a boat under the bore. Justice slows to the pace of carbon paper, and the petitioners squat in the verandah a day longer for it. Simla, receiving its forms punctually, writes Chhota Nagra down a model district.

choices.label: Have Ram Autar fill them in plausibly and file the rest.
choices.outcome: ‘It shall be done,’ says Ram Autar, and the office breathes again. The forms go up to Simla punctual and beautifully imagined. He will make the paper the Empire wants, and you will not ask how; that bargain is worth more to you than a settlement officer.

choices.label: Write to Simla objecting to Form XIV-B on principle.
choices.outcome: In a month comes Form XIV-B-1, a supplementary form for the recording of objections to Form XIV-B. Ram Autar lays it beside the first without a word.

title: Ram Autar Has a Nephew
body: Ram Autar comes at the matter as a pilot takes a shoal, by many soundings. His sister's son, it appears, is a young man of promise and good English handwriting; and there is, as it happens, a vacancy in the tahsil office. ‘Only if the Presence thinks fit,’ he says, studying the window. Half the work of the district runs on such small arrangements. You are beginning to learn how much.

choices.label: Appoint the nephew. Ram Autar has earned it.
choices.outcome: The nephew is appointed, and proves a good clerk — they always do. And you have learned how the district is really staffed. The answer is not in the Civil List; it is in Ram Autar's head, with much else.

choices.label: Insist on open competition for the post.
choices.outcome: An open examination is held, with notices in two bazaars. The nephew wins it, no other serious candidate having found it convenient to sit. You have kept the rule, spent a friendship you could ill afford, and got the same clerk either way.

title: A Letter from the Hills
body: The hot weather is on, the plains lie white as an ash-pit, and your wife of a few months has gone up to the hill station with the rest of the newly-married, as a bride must who is not to be buried on the plains before October. A letter comes down by every dak, written brighter than she feels, asking — not for the first time — when you will take your local leave, and whether the district cannot govern itself for one fortnight. The envelope smells faintly of pine.

choices.label: Take your local leave and go up to her.
choices.outcome: A fortnight of deodars and cold nights and a wife still new enough to be a wonder, and of not saying the word ‘district’ at breakfast. You come down brown, mended, and a little guilty. The files have waited. Files always wait.

choices.label: Stay at your post; the season is too dangerous to leave.
choices.outcome: You write that duty holds you to the plains, which is true, and that you will come up the moment it eases, which you both doubt. A marriage of four months learns, in one hot weather apart, the shape of the marriage it is going to be. You go back to the files.

choices.label: Stay, and put her off with a warm, evasive letter.
choices.outcome: You fill a page with the leave you mean to take and cannot name a date for, and send it up the hill. Nothing is settled. Outside the loo is blowing, and the mango-tops thrash grey with dust.

title: The Hot Weather
body: By May the thermometer stands at a hundred and ten in the shade, the station has half-emptied for the hills, and the nights are worse than the days. This is the season that breaks men quietly: the loo by day, the glare off the courtyard, and after dark the long empty evenings when the punkah creaks and there is nothing between you and the silence but a bottle and the ceiling-cloth.

choices.label: Keep to a rigid routine — dawn rides, cold baths, work.
choices.outcome: You ride at five, before the sun clears the mango-tope, take your bath cold, and work through the shuttered day by timetable. It is joyless, and it answers.

choices.label: Let the Club and the bottle carry you through.
choices.outcome: The half-dozen left in the station close ranks at the Club bar, and the same four stories go round with the ice. The evenings pass easier; the mornings, harder. It is a well-worn road, and every man on it knows where it goes.

choices.label: Drive yourself at the work to fill the emptiness.
choices.outcome: You bury the silence under files and clear arrears two years deep. Simla minutes its approval. One morning you catch sight of yourself in the shaving-glass, and pause.

title: Lala Hukum Chand Calls It In
body: The mangoes are long eaten, and the Lala has come for his return on them. Nothing so gross as the money, he protests, hands spread: merely a rival grain-dealer whose licence, looked at closely, might be found irregular. ‘A small matter,’ he says, ‘between friends.’ Through the window the bazaar goes about its business, not knowing which of you it belongs to.

choices.label: Do the small thing he asks. It is small.
choices.outcome: The licence is found wanting; a line in the Lala's ledger is scored through. It was a small matter, as he said. They are all small matters, one after another, each a little easier than the last.

choices.label: Refuse him, and let the debt stand.
choices.outcome: ‘As the Presence pleases,’ says the Lala, and the warmth goes out of the room like a lamp turned down. The debt is called to the last anna, and his money leaves the wheels of your district dry overnight. You have kept your izzat. It is not a cheap thing to keep.

choices.label: Repay him in full from the chest and be free.
choices.outcome: You pay him out of the chest — a dangerous share of it — and are quit. The Lala counts nothing and bows very low; the debt was worth more to him than the silver, and the bow says so. You walk back through the record-room a poorer man, and a free one.

title: The District Stops Work
body: What began with Pandit Girdhari's banned meeting has become a hartal in the name of the non-co-operation movement. The cloth-shops are shuttered, the courts stand empty, and your own cutcherry peons discover sick grandmothers in distant villages. Not a stone thrown, not a voice raised; only the bazaar gone silent as a tank at noon. A riot could at least be charged. This cannot.

choices.label: Break the strike under the emergency powers.
choices.outcome: You take the emergency powers, lift the organisers before dawn, and have the shops open by persuasion of the lathi. The surface of things is restored. But the district has learned that it can stop — all of it, together — and no ordinance reaches that.

choices.label: Wait it out and let the hartal exhaust itself.
choices.outcome: For eleven days you do nothing, in the grand manner, while the telegrams from Simla climb from Urgent to Clear-the-Line. On the twelfth the shops open of themselves, the point having been made. Blyth-Curram will remember that you sat still. So will the Pandit.

choices.label: Meet the Pandit and offer a real concession.
choices.outcome: You send for the Pandit and treat with him as a man with a case, which Simla does not forgive. A committee, a hearing, one grievance honestly taken up — and next morning the shutters rattle up all down the Sadar Bazaar. ‘It needed only asking,’ says the Pandit. You have kept your district. What it has cost you will arrive later, by post.

title: What Ram Autar Knew
body: An anonymous petition, in a fair court-hand, sets out with dates and figures how the head clerk's little arrangements have grown across the years into what an auditor would call embezzlement and the bazaar calls dastur. Ram Autar has run your office, saved your name a dozen times, and taken his tithe of all that passed the desk. He stands now by the almirah, still as a heron, waiting for the hukm.

choices.label: Bury the petition. He has earned that much.
choices.outcome: The petition goes into the brazier, curls once, and is gone. The office runs on. You did not buy Ram Autar's loyalty, you find; you rented it, and this is a quarter's rent. Next morning he pours out your tea as he always does, and does not ask you to meet his eye.

choices.label: Confront him privately and demand it stop.
choices.outcome: You put it to him with the doors shut. He neither denies nor excuses. ‘It shall cease,’ he says gravely, and it ceases. So does much of the ease with which your office used to run, for the two flowed in one channel.

choices.label: Report him. The law is the law.
choices.outcome: You report him, which is clean, correct, and ruinous. Ram Autar is suspended pending enquiry, and within a fortnight you learn how much of the district lived in his head and nowhere else on paper. The files are honest now, and three weeks behind.

title: A Letter from Home
body: The news came with the first rains and is only now sinking in: your wife is with child, and has gone Home for her confinement, as the wives of this Service go — to doctors who do not lose them, and fields that are green. She will be away the better part of a year. Her letter is all courage and lists of linen. Under it lies the thing you both now carry: your child will be born eleven thousand miles off, and learn your face from a photograph on the mantel.

choices.label: Write back at once, warmly, and promise you will get Home.
choices.outcome: You fill a page with a furlough not yet sanctioned and an English April you can barely call to mind. It steadies you to write it. Whether the promise lives through the Secretariat’s leave-list is next year’s grief.

choices.label: Send money, and a correct, contained letter of good wishes.
choices.outcome: You do as the Service does: provide handsomely and show nothing. The draft goes by the same mail as a letter warm enough to pass and cool enough to leave you fit for work, and you seal it knowing what it is. Outside, the rain drums on the thatch.

choices.label: Pour a drink and leave it a day, then a week.
choices.outcome: You mean to answer it to-morrow. To-morrow there is a breach in the canal bund, and the day after a dacoity, and the letter goes into the drawer with the others. The silence between you and a family you have not met grows by one more mail.
